```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
#install.packages("rmarkdown")
```

When you estimate parameters in linear regression, you are trying to find the value that, when used in conjunction with the independent variables, returns a line that best represents the data that you are working with. The so-called "line of best fit". There are several ways to estimate the value of the parameters that define that line. The simplest (and most frequently taught) is to draw a straight line through the data, and then "rotate" it until the difference between the observed data and the line, with respect to the y axis, is minimised. This is usually quantified by squaring this vertical distance and squaring it (to account for negative values). In essence, this "rotation" of the line is equivalent to trying out a number of parameters, and then minimising the sum of squares, which tells us the quality of the fit. The smallest value for the sum of squares is expected to return the best estimates for the parameters that explain the data. You can see a manual calculation for this value using an analytical approach in my [ordinary least squares](https://github.com/PlantsGenesBugs/OLS_parameter_estimation) repo, and an alternative way for parameter optimisation in my [maximum likelihood estimation](https://github.com/PlantsGenesBugs/Max_Likelihood_Estimation) repo. 

In this file I will be using a fourth method called **gradient descent**. Gradient descent is a method that aims to find the "line of best fit" by minimising a value that assesses the quality of that fit (somewhat like finding the smallest sum of squares). The value we will be using is the mean square error (MSE), and in this context it is also called the cost function. This is the value we want to minimise. The mean square error is essentially the residual sum of squares divided by 2n:

\[
\frac{1}{2n}(y - X\beta)^T(y - X\beta)
\]

The algorithm works by repeatedly adjusting the model parameters, based on the direction of steepest decrease in the cost function. This iterative approach helps the model converge toward the optimal solution, taking the following steps:  

1. Initial values are (randomly) assigned to the parameters for our parameters.
2. A learning rate (alpha) is set. This value controls the size of the jump during the iterative process (the size of change in parameter values between iterative cycles). 
3. The parameters are iteratively updated using the following formula: 

\[
\beta^{(j+1)} = \beta^{(j)} - \alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta^{(j)}} J(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p) = \beta^{(j)} - \alpha \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} [y_i - f(\underline{x}_i)] x_{ij}
\]

The current parameter is adjusted by subtracting the learning rate multiplied by the gradient (partial derivative) of the cost function. This calculation is preformed for one variable at a time, and each one is updated after every iterative round.  
4. The process is stopped once it reaches a pre-defined stopping rule. This could be the number of iterations or when the difference between the value of the cost function for the two most recent rounds falls underneath a prescribed threshold.

The learning rate and stopping rule are also known as hyperparameters. These can be optimised to ensure accurate estimation. For example, for the learning rate different values (0.1, 0.01. and 0.001) can be used to test the difference. 

```{r}
# load all required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

# download data from Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/jvikumyasarathne/renewable-energy-data-set/data
# or download using RKaggle
#install.packages("RKaggle")
#library(RKaggle)

# renewables_data <- RKaggle::get_dataset("jakewright/house-price-data")


renewables_data <- read_excel("Renewable_Energy_Dataset.xlsx")

# plan is to use wind energy data, split by onshore/offshore, model one, then model other to compare
# model daily energy output by wind speed

onshore_wind <- renewables_data %>%
  filter(Technology_Type == "Wind Onshore")

offshore_wind <- renewables_data %>%
  filter(Technology_Type == "Wind Offshore")


ggplot(renewables_data, aes(x = Equipment_Age_Years, y = Daily_Energy_Output_MWh)) +
    geom_point()

renewables_data %>% filter(Technology_Type=="Solar PV") %>% filter(Daily_Energy_Output_MWh<800) %>% filter(Daily_Energy_Output_MWh>100) %>% ggplot(aes(x = Solar_Irradiance_kWh_m2, y = Daily_Energy_Output_MWh)) +
    geom_point()

df <- renewables_data %>% filter(Technology_Type=="Solar PV") %>% filter(Daily_Energy_Output_MWh>800 | Daily_Energy_Output_MWh<100)
m <- lm(Daily_Energy_Output_MWh ~ Solar_Irradiance_kWh_m2, data=df)
summary(m)

y <- df$Daily_Energy_Output_MWh
x <- df$Solar_Irradiance_kWh_m2

```
Here we want to minimise (optimise) the cost function, represented by the Mean Squared Error. We start by choosing the initial parameters and then iterating over the cost function, using gradient descent to choose the next value(s) of the variables per iteration. To note: optimisation algorithms don’t always produce the same results for all choices of initialisations.  

```{r}
cost_fn <- function(X, y, coef) {
    sum( (X %*% coef - y)^2 ) / (2*length(y))
}

# First we set alpha and the number of iterations we will perform
alpha <- 0.05
num_iters <- 2000

# next we will initialise regression coefficients; start all at 0.1
coef <- matrix(c(0.1,0.1), nrow=2)
X <- cbind(1, matrix(x))
res <- vector("list", num_iters)


for (i in 1:num_iters) {
  error <- (X %*% coef - y)
  delta <- t(X) %*% error / length(y)
  coef <- coef - alpha * delta
  res_df <- data.frame(itr = i , cost = cost_fn(X, y, coef),
                   b0 = coef[1], b1 = coef[2])

  res[[i]] <- res_df
}


```

Combine all results into a simple data frame. If we look at the final values in the resulting variable we see that b0 and b1 seem to have converged on fixed values.

```{r}
res_df <- bind_rows(res)
tail(res_df)
```
We can look at the convergence of the parameters, the cost function itself or even the estimated y at each step of the optimisation.

```{r}
ggplot(res_df, aes(x = itr, y = b1)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(x = "Iteration",
         y = "Estimated beta_1",
         title = "Visualisation of the cconvergence of the beta_1 parameter")

```
We can also compare the values we have determined by gradient descent to those predicted by linear modeling. 

```{r linear_model}
fit <- lm(y ~ x)

coef(fit)

```
These are quite close, so our approach has worked. However, to illustrate how sensitive gradient descent is to the starting conditions, I will show you my initial results below, showing the effect of a step size that is too big: the value for the coefficient doesn't converge and swings wildly between two extremes.

```{r}
# Set alpha and the number of iterations we will perform
alpha <- 0.1
num_iters <- 100

# Initialise regression coefficients; start all at 0.1
coef <- matrix(c(0.1,0.1), nrow=2)
X <- cbind(1, matrix(x))
res <- vector("list", num_iters)


for (i in 1:num_iters) {
  error <- (X %*% coef - y)
  delta <- t(X) %*% error / length(y)
  coef <- coef - alpha * delta
  res_df <- data.frame(itr = i , cost = cost_fn(X, y, coef),
                   b0 = coef[1], b1 = coef[2])

  res[[i]] <- res_df
}

res_df <- bind_rows(res)

ggplot(res_df, aes(x = itr, y = b1)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(x = "Iteration",
         y = "Estimated beta_1",
         title = "Visualisation of the cconvergence of the beta_1 parameter")

```
There is a way to calculate a suitable alpha. This depends on the number of observations and the largest eigenvalue. The largest eigenvalue measures the maximum curvature of the quadratic function associated with the matrix \(X^\top X/n\). It can therefore be used to determine a suitable learning rate for gradient-based optimisation.

```{r calulate_alpha}
n <- length(y)

lambda_max <- max(
  eigen(crossprod(X) / n,
        symmetric = TRUE,
        only.values = TRUE)$values
)

alpha_max <- 2 / lambda_max

c(alpha_max = alpha_max, current_alpha = alpha)

```
